prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), what is the slope of the secant through inputs \(4\) and \(4+h\), before taking the limit? Assume \(h\ne0\) and \(4+h\) is in the domain.
why: Multiply \((\sqrt{9+h}-3)/h\) by its conjugate over itself. The new numerator is \(h\), which cancels.

prompt: For the lecture graph \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), where does the tangent at \(x=4\) cross the horizontal axis?
why: Rationalizing the difference quotient gives slope \(1/6\) at \((4,3)\). Set \(0-3=(x-4)/6\) and solve.

prompt: A line through \((4,3)\) is tangent to \(y=\sqrt{x+5}\) there. Which identity gives its exact vertical distance above the graph for a nearby input \(4+h\)?
why: Write \(\sqrt{9+h}-3=h/(\sqrt{9+h}+3)\). Subtraction leaves \(h(\sqrt{9+h}-3)/[6(\sqrt{9+h}+3)]\). Rationalize once more.

prompt: Set \(f(x)=(x+1)^2\) for \(x\ne-1\) but \(f(-1)=1\). What are the left and right limits, respectively, of the difference quotient defining \(f'(-1)\)?
why: For \(h\ne0\) the quotient is \((h^2-1)/h=h-1/h\). Its one-sided limits have opposite signs.

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+6}\), use the tangent at \(x=3\) to estimate \(f(3.12)\). Which estimate and slope go together?
why: The point is \((3,3)\) and the derivative there is \(1/6\). The tangent predicts an increase of \(0.12/6=0.02\).

prompt: Keep \(f(x)=(x+1)^2\) to the left of \(-1\). To the right, including \(-1\), use \(f(x)=m(x+1)+b\). Which pair makes \(f\) differentiable at \(-1\)?
why: Continuity forces \(b=0\). The left difference quotient is \(h\), with limit zero, while the right quotient is \(m\). Matching slopes forces \(m=0\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), the secant over \([a,a+h]\) has slope \(3-2a-h\). At what input is the instantaneous slope equal to that secant slope?
why: Differentiate to get \(f'(c)=3-2c\). Equating the two slopes gives \(2c=2a+h\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), the tangent at \(x=a\) is measured again at \(x=a+h\). How much higher than the graph is the tangent there?
why: Expand \(f(a+h)=f(a)+(3-2a)h-h^2\). The first two terms give the tangent height, so the difference is \(h^2\).

prompt: A particle has \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\) on \([0,4]\). On which open intervals does it speed up?
why: Velocity is \(3(t-1)(t-3)\) and acceleration is \(6(t-2)\). Their signs agree precisely on \((1,2)\) and \((3,4)\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\), what happens as time passes through \(t=2\)?
choices: Motion stays negative while speed changes from increasing to decreasing.
Motion reverses from negative to positive.
Motion stays positive while speed reaches a minimum.
The particle is momentarily at rest with nonzero acceleration.
why: Velocity is \(-3\) at \(t=2\) and stays negative nearby. Acceleration changes from negative to positive, so speed has a local maximum.

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\) meters on \([0,4]\), find total distance and displacement, respectively.
why: Velocity changes sign at \(1,3\). The successive positions are \(2,6,2,6\), so distance is \(4+4+4\) and displacement is \(6-2\).

prompt: A ball has height \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\) feet until impact. What are its average velocity over the flight and its velocity just before impact, respectively?
why: The physical root of \(H(t)=0\) is \(t=2\). The secant slope is \((0-96)/2=-48\), and \(H'(2)=-16-32(2)=-80\).

prompt: A car follows \(s(t)=t^2-2t-3\) feet for \(t\ge0\). At which times, and with which velocities, does it pass position \(-3\) ft?
why: Set \(t^2-2t=0\) to find both admissible times. Substituting each into \(2t-2\) gives opposite velocities.

prompt: For the same flight model \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\), at what height is the downward speed exactly half its impact speed?
why: Impact occurs at \(t=2\), so the impact speed is \(80\). Solve \(16+32t=40\) to get \(t=3/4\). Then \(H(3/4)=96-12-9=75\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\) on \([0,5]\), when is the particle moving left and speeding up?
why: Moving left and speeding up requires both \(v=-3(t-2)(t-4)<0\) and \(a=-6(t-3)<0\). Only \((4,5)\) satisfies both.

prompt: For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\) on \([0,5]\), which instants are reversals, and which instant changes acceleration sign without a reversal?
choices: Reversals at \(2,4\); acceleration changes sign at \(3\).
Reversal at \(3\); acceleration changes sign at \(2,4\).
Reversals at \(2,3,4\); acceleration never changes sign.
Reversal at \(4\) only; acceleration changes sign at \(2\).
why: Velocity is \(-3(t-2)(t-4)\) and changes sign at both roots. Acceleration vanishes at \(3\), where velocity is positive.

prompt: For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\) meters on \([0,5]\), what is average speed?
why: At times \(0,2,4,5\) the positions are \(5,-15,-11,-15\). Total distance is \(20+4+4=28\) meters over five seconds.

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\) on \([0,4]\), at which two times is the instantaneous velocity equal to the average velocity over the full interval?
why: Average velocity is \((6-2)/4=1\). Solve \(3(t-2)^2-3=1\) to obtain both times.

prompt: For \(f(x)=\lvert x\rvert\), the secant joining \(-h\) to \(h\) has slope zero for every \(h>0\). Why does this fail to give \(f'(0)=0\)?
choices: The secants from \(0\) to \(h\) and from \(0\) to \(-h\) have different limiting slopes.
The derivative is zero because all symmetric secants are horizontal.
The derivative is one because the graph lies above the horizontal axis.
The derivative fails because the function is discontinuous at zero.
why: The derivative requires the difference quotient based at \(0\). It equals \(1\) on the right and \(-1\) on the left, while the symmetric quotient always compares equal heights.

prompt: For the lecture parabola \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), which two lines through \((0,1)\) are tangent to the graph?
why: At \(a\) the slope is \(3-2a\). The tangent is \(y=(3-2a)x+a^2\). Its intercept is \(1\) when \(a=\pm1\), giving slopes \(1,5\).

prompt: A differentiable position function satisfies \(s'(2)=-4\). What is \(\lim_{h\to0}[s(2+2h)-s(2-h)]/h\)?
why: Insert \(s(2)\) between the two terms. The forward increment divided by \(h\) tends to \(2s'(2)\), and the backward difference divided by \(h\) tends to \(s'(2)\). Add the limits.

prompt: For the lecture function \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), pick the value of \(h\ne0\) for which the secant from \(4\) to \(4+h\) has slope \(1/7\).
why: Rationalization gives the secant slope \(1/(\sqrt{9+h}+3)\). Equate the denominator to \(7\) and solve \(\sqrt{9+h}=4\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), evaluate \([f(a+h)-2f(a)+f(a-h)]/h^2\) for \(h\ne0\).
why: The linear terms in \(h\) cancel when \(f(a+h)\) and \(f(a-h)\) are added. Each contributes \(-h^2\), leaving the exact quotient \(-2\).

prompt: Suppose \(f(1)=3\) and \(f'(1)=-2\). Evaluate \(\lim_{h\to0}[f(1+h)^2-9]/h\).
why: Factor the numerator into \([f(1+h)-3][f(1+h)+3]\). The first factor divided by \(h\) tends to \(-2\). Differentiability gives continuity, so the second tends to \(6\).

prompt: A car has \(s(t)=t^2-2t-3\) feet for \(t\ge0\). Find its average velocity between passing the origin and reaching \(s=5\) ft.
why: The physical solutions of \(s(t)=0\) and \(s(t)=5\) are \(3\) and \(4\) seconds. The car changes position by \(5\) ft in \(1\) second.

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), what is the slope of the secant joining \((1,2)\) and \((2,2)\)?
why: Both points are at height \(2\). The change in height divided by the change in input is zero.

prompt: A secant to \(f(x)=3x-x^2\) runs from \(x=1\) to \(x=1.5\). What horizontal change belongs in the denominator of its slope?
why: Subtract the starting input from the ending input to get \(1.5-1=0.5\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), which expression gives the secant slope between \(1\) and a different input \(x\)?
why: Factor \(3x-x^2-2=-(x-1)(x-2)\), then divide by \(x-1\).

prompt: The graph of \(f(x)=mx+b\) has what instantaneous slope at \(x=2\)?
why: The slope of a line is constant. Its difference quotient is \(mh/h=m\) for \(h\ne0\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), what point on the graph do you use when forming the tangent at \(x=4\)?
why: Evaluate \(f(4)=\sqrt9=3\) and put the input first in the ordered pair.

prompt: For \(f(x)=\lvert x\rvert\), what are the right-hand and left-hand slopes at zero, in that order?
why: For \(h>0\), \(\lvert h\rvert/h=1\). For \(h<0\), \(\lvert h\rvert/h=-1\).

prompt: The first derivative of \(f(x)=3x-x^2\) is \(3-2x\). What is \(f''(x)\)?
why: The constant \(3\) differentiates to zero and the derivative of \(-2x\) is \(-2\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), which is its third derivative?
why: Its second derivative is the constant \(-2\). The derivative of a constant is zero.

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), at which input does the graph have horizontal tangent line \(y=9/4\)?
why: Set \(3-2x=0\), which gives \(x=3/2\). Substitution into the original function gives \(9/2-9/4=9/4\).

prompt: If \(y=f(x)\), which notation means the same thing as \(f'''(x)\)?
why: The superscripts in the third derivative notation count differentiations with respect to \(x\).

prompt: In \(\lim_{h\to0}[(1+h)^2-1]/h\), if \(f(x)=x^2\), which input and derivative value does the quotient describe?
why: The numerator is \(f(1+h)-f(1)\). Expanding gives \(2h+h^2\), so the quotient tends to \(2\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+6}\), which line is tangent to the graph at \(x=3\)?
why: The point is \((3,3)\) and rationalizing the difference quotient gives slope \(1/6\). Expand \(y-3=(x-3)/6\).

prompt: A function equals \((x+1)^2\) except that \(f(-1)=1\). What makes it discontinuous at \(-1\)?
choices: The limit is \(0\) and the function value is \(1\).
The limit is \(1\) and the function value is \(0\).
The left limit is \(-1\) and the right limit is \(1\).
The function has no value at \(-1\).
why: Nearby values are \((x+1)^2\), which approach \(0\). The assigned height at \(-1\) is \(1\).

prompt: A particle has position \(s(t)=3t-t^2\) meters. What is its velocity at \(t=1\) second?
why: Differentiate to get \(v(t)=3-2t\), and substitute \(t=1\).

prompt: If velocity is \(-3\) m/s at an instant, what is the speed?
why: Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so take the absolute value.

prompt: For \(s(t)=3t-t^2\) meters, when is the particle momentarily at rest?
why: Rest means zero velocity. Solving \(3-2t=0\) gives \(t=3/2\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=3t-t^2\), what happens on \(3/2<t<3\)?
choices: It travels in the negative direction and speeds up.
It travels in the negative direction and slows down.
It travels in the positive direction and speeds up.
why: Velocity \(3-2t\) is negative and acceleration is \(-2\). They have the same sign, so the magnitude of the velocity increases.

prompt: The height of the ball is \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\) ft. Which equation finds the instant it hits the ground?
why: Ground contact specifies a height of zero. Time is measured from release, so only nonnegative roots describe this flight.

prompt: For \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\) feet, what is the physical impact time?
why: Ground contact requires \(-16(t+3)(t-2)=0\). Only \(t=2\) lies in the flight interval.

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^2-2t-3\) feet with \(t\ge0\), what is the velocity at the instant the car passes position \(5\) ft?
For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\) meters, what is the acceleration at \(t=2\) s?
why: Differentiate twice to get \(a(t)=-6t+18\). At \(t=2\), this is \(6\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=3t-t^2\) on \(0\le t\le3\), what is the total length of time for which speed exceeds \(2\) m/s?
why: Solve \(\lvert3-2t\rvert>2\). On the physical interval this gives \(0\le t<1/2\) and \(5/2<t\le3\). Each interval lasts half a second.

prompt: For the falling ball \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\) feet, determine its downward speed at the instant it has fallen exactly half its initial height.
why: Set \(H(t)=48\) to get \(t^2+t=3\). The positive value of \(2t+1\) satisfies \((2t+1)^2=13\). During the flight the speed is \(16(2t+1)\).

prompt: On \(y=3x-x^2\) the endpoints of a secant are at \(x=1\) and \(x=b\). Which \(b\ne1\) gives a secant parallel to \(y=5-2x\)?
why: The secant slope from \(1\) to \(b\) simplifies to \(2-b\). Equating it to \(-2\) gives \(b=4\).

prompt: The secant of \(y=3x-x^2\) through the points at \(x=0,3\) is horizontal. How far above that line is the parallel tangent?
why: The secant is \(y=0\). A parallel tangent has \(3-2x=0\), hence height \(3(3/2)-(3/2)^2=9/4\).

prompt: On \(y=3x-x^2\), draw tangents at the two zeros. Where do those tangents intersect?
why: At \(x=0,3\) the slopes are \(3,-3\). The tangents are \(y=3x\) and \(y=-3(x-3)\). Set them equal to obtain the intersection.

prompt: How many different tangent lines to \(y=3x-x^2\) pass through the point \((1,1)\)?
why: The tangent at \(a\) is \(y=(3-2a)x+a^2\). At \(x=1\) its height is \(2+(a-1)^2\), at least \(2\). It therefore cannot pass through \((1,1)\).

prompt: Suppose \(f(3)=5\) and \(f'(3)=-2\). Which limit is determined by these data: \(\lim_{x\to3}[f(x)-5]/(x^2-9)\)?
why: Factor \(x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)\). The first quotient tends to \(f'(3)=-2\), then divide by the limit \(6\).

prompt: Suppose \(f'(a)=3\). What is \(\lim_{h\to0}[f(a+h^2)-f(a)]/h\)?
why: Write it as \(h\) times the difference quotient with increment \(h^2\). The quotient tends to \(3\) and \(h\) tends to zero.

prompt: Suppose \(f'(a)=2\) and \(g'(a)=-3\). Find \(\lim_{x\to a}[f(x)-f(a)]/[g(x)-g(a)]\) from the definition of derivative.
choices: The values \(f(a),g(a)\) must also be known.
why: Divide both numerator and denominator by \(x-a\). The two difference quotients tend to \(2,-3\). Since the denominator limit is nonzero, their quotient tends to \(-2/3\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), compare the secant slopes from \(4\) to \(3\) and from \(4\) to \(5\), in that order, with the tangent slope at \(4\).
why: Rationalizing gives slopes \(1/(3+\sqrt8)\) and \(1/(3+\sqrt{10})\). Their denominators lie on opposite sides of \(6\).

prompt: Use the derivative definition for \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\) at its left endpoint \(x=-5\). What happens to its right-hand secant slopes?
choices: They increase without bound as the second point approaches \(-5\).
why: At an increment \(h>0\) the slope is \(\sqrt h/h=1/\sqrt h\). This grows without bound, giving a vertical endpoint tangent.

prompt: For \(g(x)=x\lvert x\rvert\), why does \(g'(0)\) exist even though the absolute-value factor has a corner?
choices: Its difference quotient at zero equals \(\lvert h\rvert\) and tends to zero.
The left and right slopes are \(-1\) and \(1\).
Every product of continuous functions is differentiable.
The difference quotient equals \(\lvert h\rvert/h\) and tends to one.
why: Since \(g(0)=0\), the quotient is \(h\lvert h\rvert/h\). Cancel the nonzero increment before taking its limit.

prompt: A line \(y=mx+b\) is tangent to \(y=\sqrt{x+5}\) at \(x=4\). What is \(m+b\)?
why: The conjugate calculation gives \(m=1/6\). Since the line contains \((4,3)\), its intercept is \(7/3\), yielding \(m+b=15/6\).

prompt: Two points on \(y=\sqrt{x+5}\) have heights \(2\) and \(4\). At what point does the tangent have the same slope as their secant?
why: The inputs are \(-1,11\), so the secant slope is \(2/12=1/6\). Rationalizing the general difference quotient gives \(f'(x)=1/[2\sqrt{x+5}]\). Setting it to \(1/6\) gives the stated point.

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+5}\), evaluate \(\lim_{h\to0}[(f(4+h)-f(4))/h-1/6]/h\).
why: The inner quotient is \(1/(\sqrt{9+h}+3)\). Subtract \(1/6\), then use \(3-\sqrt{9+h}=-h/(3+\sqrt{9+h})\). After cancellation the limit is \(-1/[6(3+3)^2]\).

prompt: Suppose a polynomial \(g\) satisfies \(g''=-2\) everywhere and \(g(0)=0\), as does the lecture parabola \(3x-x^2\). What extra datum forces those polynomials to agree?
why: A polynomial with second derivative \(-2\) and zero constant term has the form \(-x^2+bx\). Its first derivative at zero determines \(b\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), where do the graphs of \(f'\) and \(f''\) intersect?
why: Set \(3-2x=-2\) to find \(x=5/2\). Both derivative graphs have height \(-2\) there.

prompt: For \(f(x)=3x-x^2\), find all inputs where \(f(x)\) equals \(f'(x)\).
why: Set \(3x-x^2=3-2x\), giving \(x^2-5x+3=0\). Apply the quadratic formula.

prompt: Suppose \(p\) is cubic with \(p'''=6\), \(p''(0)=-2\), \(p'(0)=3\), and \(p(0)=0\). At which point do its graph and the lecture parabola \(3x-x^2\) have the same value and first two derivatives?
why: The data give \(p=x^3-x^2+3x\). Its difference from the parabola is \(x^3\), whose value and first two derivatives all vanish at \(0\) and nowhere else.

prompt: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\) and \(f(a)\ne0\), find \(\lim_{h\to0}[1/f(a+h)-1/f(a)]/h\).
why: A common denominator gives the negative difference quotient of \(f\) divided by \(f(a+h)f(a)\). By continuity the latter tends to \(f(a)^2\ne0\).
Write the expression as \([f(h)/h][g(h)/h]\). Each bracket is a difference quotient at zero, so the limits multiply.

prompt: Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(a\) with \(f'(a)=-2\). Which is the limit of \(\lvert f(a+h)-f(a)\rvert/\lvert h\rvert\) as \(h\to0\), and does \(\lvert f(a+h)-f(a)\rvert/h\) also have a two-sided limit?
choices: The first limit is \(2\). The second has no two-sided limit.
The first has no limit, and the second equals \(2\).
why: The first expression is the absolute value of the difference quotient and tends to \(2\). The second multiplies that expression by \(\lvert h\rvert/h\), which has opposite signs on the two sides.

prompt: Consider \(f(x)=(x+1)^2\) for \(x\ne-1\) and \(f(-1)=1\). At which inputs \(a\) is \(f'(a)=0\)?
why: Away from \(-1\) the derivative is \(2(x+1)\), which has no zero there. At \(-1\) the jump between the assigned height and the limiting height prevents differentiability.

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+6}\), find an input where its tangent is perpendicular to a line of slope \(-4\).
why: The desired slope is \(1/4\). The derivative \(1/(2\sqrt{x+6})\) equals \(1/4\) precisely when \(x+6=4\).

prompt: For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+6}\), the tangent at \(x=3\) estimates \(f(3+h)\) by \(3+h/6\). When \(h=7\), by how much does that estimate exceed the exact value?
why: At \(x=10\) the tangent estimate is \(25/6\) and the exact function value is \(4\). Their difference is \(1/6\).

prompt: Join \(f(x)=(x+1)^2\) for \(x\le-1\) to \(f(x)=A(x+1)^2+B(x+1)+C\) for \(x>-1\). Which coefficients make \(f\) twice differentiable at \(-1\)?
why: Continuity forces \(C=0\), and agreement of first derivatives forces \(B=0\). The left and right difference quotients of \(f'\) at the join then tend to \(2\) and \(2A\), so \(A=1\).

prompt: Let \(g(x)=x\lvert x\rvert\). Which description of differentiability at the origin is correct?
why: The first derivative is \(2\lvert x\rvert\) for \(x\ne0\), and the original difference quotient gives \(g'(0)=0\). The graph of \(g'\) therefore has left and right slopes \(-2,2\) at zero.

prompt: A product is defined by \(F(x)=\lvert x\rvert p(x)\) with \(p\) differentiable near \(0\). What condition is necessary and sufficient for \(F\) to be differentiable at \(0\)?
why: The right difference quotient tends to \(p(0)\) and the left one to \(-p(0)\) by continuity of \(p\). They are equal exactly when \(p(0)=0\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\) on \([0,4]\), which instants give the largest speed?
why: Velocity is \(3(t-2)^2-3\). Its range on the interval is \([-3,9]\), so the largest speed is \(9\) at the endpoints.

prompt: For \(s(t)=3t-t^2\) meters on \([0,3]\), compare total distance and the numerical magnitude of displacement.
choices: Distance is \(9/2\) m and displacement is \(0\) m.
Distance is \(9/4\) m and displacement is \(0\) m.
Distance and displacement are both \(9/2\) m.
why: The endpoints are both at the origin. The particle rises to \(s(3/2)=9/4\) and then returns, traveling that distance twice.

prompt: For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+2\) on \([0,4]\), at which times does the particle pass its starting position, and what happens at its last visit?
choices: \(0,3\). At \(3\) it crosses with nonzero velocity.
why: Solve \(s(t)-s(0)=t(t-3)^2=0\). At the repeated root \(3\), \(v=3(t-1)(t-3)\) changes from negative to positive.

prompt: For the car \(s(t)=t^2-2t-3\) on \(t\ge0\), which positions occur at two distinct nonnegative times?
why: Rewrite as \(s=(t-1)^2-4\). Distinct times are \(1\pm\sqrt{s+4}\). Both are nonnegative exactly when \(0<s+4\le1\).

prompt: A ball falls according to \(H(t)=96-16t-16t^2\). How far does it fall during the last half second before impact?
why: Impact is at \(2\) seconds. Half a second earlier its height was \(96-16(1.5)-16(1.5)^2=36\) ft, which it loses by impact.

prompt: For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\), what is the displacement from the first direction reversal to the next?
why: The velocity \(-3(t-2)(t-4)\) changes sign at \(2,4\). Subtract \(s(2)=-15\) from \(s(4)=-11\).

prompt: For \(s(t)=-t^3+9t^2-24t+5\) on \([0,5]\), at which time after the first reversal does the particle first return to the position of that reversal?
choices: It never returns on this interval.
why: The first reversal is at \(2\) and \(s(2)=-15\). Solve \(s(t)+15=-(t-2)^2(t-5)=0\). The root greater than \(2\) is \(5\).
